title: Jump Game
directAnswer: Each value is the max jump length from that index; decide whether you can reach the last index. The DP answer marks which indices are 'good' (can reach the end) in O(n²). The optimal greedy does it in one pass: track the farthest index reachable so far, and if you ever stand on an index beyond that reach, you're stuck. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy reachability — track farthest reachable index
remember.formula:
farthest = 0
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    if i > farthest: return False   # stranded before reaching i
    farthest = max(farthest, i + x)
return True
rules: Carry a single number **`farthest`** = the maximum index reachable using everything seen so far.
Before processing index `i`, if **`i > farthest`** you can never stand on `i` → return `False` immediately.
At each reachable `i`, update **`farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`** — the new horizon.
You don't need to track exact jump sequences — only the **frontier of reachability** matters, which is why greedy beats DP here.
Early-out the moment `farthest >= n - 1` if you like; reaching the end means success regardless of what's after.
whenToUse: Reachability / feasibility on a line where each position grants a forward range
You only need yes/no (or a min count), not the actual path taken
A local 'how far can I get' frontier can be extended greedily left to right
Each step's options are a contiguous prefix of future indices (a jump *up to* k)
antiSignals: You must return the actual jump path → augment with parent pointers, not bare greedy
Jumps can go backward or costs vary per edge → model as a graph + BFS/Dijkstra
Minimum number of jumps with non-uniform structure → Jump Game II (still greedy, but level-by-level)
Ranges aren't contiguous prefixes (arbitrary reachable sets) → general graph reachability
remember.takeaway: Jump Game is the cleanest 'reachability frontier' greedy: one variable, one pass, and the key realisation that you never need the route — only whether the horizon ever falls behind you. The same farthest-reach trick scales to Jump Game II (count jumps) and Gas Station (circular feasibility).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that this feasibility question doesn't need a path or a full DP — that a single greedy 'farthest reachable' frontier captures everything — and whether you can argue why the greedy is correct, not just that it passes.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Over-engineering with O(n²) DP or recursion that TLEs, or in the greedy version checking i > farthest in the wrong place (after updating) so a stranded index slips through.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Present the DP first to show you can model it, then collapse to the O(n) greedy and justify it: a contiguous reachable prefix means the only thing that can stop you is the frontier failing to advance past your current position.

problemStatement:
You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the array's **first index**, and each element in the array represents your **maximum jump length** at that position.

Return `true` if you can reach the ***last index***, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: From index i you may jump to any index in [i+1, i+nums[i]]
understanding: Standing on index 0, each cell tells you the maximum number of steps you may hop forward from it (0 means you're stuck there). Decide whether some sequence of hops lands you on — or past — the final index. You don't need the route, just whether one exists.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a jump be shorter than the value, or must I jump exactly nums[i]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most nums[i] — any length from 1 up to nums[i]. That 'up to' is why the reachable set from i is a contiguous prefix, which the greedy exploits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does a 0 mean?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You can't move from that index. A 0 is only fatal if it's a position you're forced to stop on with no reach beyond it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the path or just whether it's reachable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just a boolean for LeetCode 55. The minimum number of jumps is the follow-up, Jump Game II.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array have a single element?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — [0] returns true because you're already on the last index. The greedy handles this since farthest starts at 0 = last index.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index. (Or jump 2 from index 0, etc.)
You always land on index 3 (value 0) at best, and can't move past it to reach index 4.
Already on the last (and only) index — no jump needed.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both solve the feasibility question; the greedy realises you only ever need the reachability frontier.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming — Mark the 'Good' Indices
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this to show you can model reachability formally, then call out the O(n²) cost as the reason to look for something better.
hints: Call an index 'good' if you can reach the last index from it. The last index is trivially good — work backward from there.
Index i is good if some j in [i+1, i+nums[i]] is already known to be good. How would you check that?
Fill a boolean dp array right to left; for each i scan its reachable range for any good index. Answer is dp[0].
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n indices we may scan up to its full jump range looking for a good index, so the worst case is O(n²) time; the boolean dp array uses O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Define `dp[i] = true` if the last index is reachable starting from `i`. The last index is good by definition. Process indices from right to left; `i` is good if any index within its jump range `[i+1, i+nums[i]]` is already marked good.

**Why work right to left.** Reachability composes backward: 'can I finish from `i`?' depends on whether I can hop to some position that itself can finish. By filling from the end, every index in `i`'s reach has already been decided, so the lookup is a simple scan over a settled region.

**Why scan the whole reachable range.** From `i` you may land on any index up to `i + nums[i]`. If *even one* of those is good, then `i` is good — you'd jump there and let it carry you home. So we OR together the goodness of the reachable window. The moment we find a good target we can stop scanning that window.

**Why we don't ship this.** That inner scan over each index's range is what makes it quadratic. For `n = 10⁴` that's up to 10⁸ checks — borderline and wasteful when the structure is so simple. The DP is a great way to *prove* the recurrence and to convince yourself reachability is well-defined, but the next observation collapses all that scanning into a single number.
approaches.insight: The DP exposes the key fact the greedy will exploit: goodness only ever propagates *backward* from a contiguous good region near the end. Once you notice the good indices form a single growing suffix-frontier (not scattered islands), you realise you never needed an array of booleans — just the boundary of that frontier.

dryRun.intro: Mark dp from the right. dp[last] = true; each i is good if its range hits a good index.

java.explanation: The last index can trivially reach itself — the base case the recurrence builds on.
Right to left, so every index in i's reach is already decided.
Clamp the jump range to the array bounds.
If any reachable index is good, i is good — stop scanning this window.
Can we finish from the start? That's the whole question.

python.explanation: Last index is good by definition.
Fill backward so lookups read settled values.
A single good target in range makes i good.

edgeCases.behavior: n=1 so dp[0] is set true by the base case and the loop never runs → returns true.
dp[3]'s only reach is index 3+0=3 (itself); it stays false, and that falseness propagates back to dp[0] → false.

pitfalls: Forgetting to clamp i + nums[i] to n-1 — out-of-bounds on large jump values.
Filling dp left to right — you'd read undecided cells.
Shipping the O(n²) version when n = 10⁴ makes the greedy clearly preferable.

approaches.name: Greedy — Track the Farthest Reachable Index (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'I only need the frontier of reachability — one number, one pass' and justify why that's sufficient.
hints: Instead of asking 'is each index good?', ask one running question: what's the farthest index I can possibly reach so far?
Sweep left to right. If you ever arrive at an index i that's beyond your current farthest reach, no jump sequence could have put you there — fail.
Otherwise extend the frontier: farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]). If you finish the sweep (or farthest covers the end), you succeed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass with O(1) work per element (one comparison, one max) gives O(n) time, and we keep just one integer farthest, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain `farthest` = the largest index reachable using all the jumps considered so far. Scan left to right. At index `i`, if `i > farthest` you could never have stepped onto `i`, so return `false`. Otherwise extend the frontier with `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. Survive the whole scan and you can reach the end.

**Why one number captures everything.** From index `i` you can land on *any* index up to `i + nums[i]` — a contiguous block, not a scattered set. That means the set of all reachable indices is itself always a contiguous prefix `[0, farthest]`; there are never gaps. So 'which exact indices are reachable' is fully described by a single boundary, `farthest`. We don't need a boolean array or a path — just the right edge of the reachable interval.

**Why `i > farthest` is the only failure mode.** As long as `i <= farthest`, index `i` lies inside the reachable prefix, so we genuinely can stand there, and from there we get to push the frontier further. The only way to fail is to reach an `i` that the frontier hasn't covered — meaning every earlier index's reach died out before `i`, the classic 'trapped behind a 0' situation. Detecting that one condition is the entire algorithm.

**Why the greedy is provably correct, not just lucky.** Because the reachable region is a contiguous prefix, extending `farthest` greedily at every reachable index can never miss an option: any index we *could* reach, we *do* account for, since its whole jump range is within `[i+1, i+nums[i]]` and `i` is already inside the frontier. There's no future decision that a different earlier choice would have unlocked — the maximum frontier dominates all alternatives. That domination argument is what turns a heuristic into a correct greedy.

**Why this beats the DP outright.** The DP rediscovers reachability by scanning each index's range; the greedy folds all of that into a single running maximum, dropping O(n²) to O(n) and O(n) space to O(1). Same answer, none of the bookkeeping.
approaches.insight: The mental shift is from 'compute goodness for every index' to 'maintain the right edge of where I can be'. Once you see that 'jump up to k' makes the reachable set a gap-free interval, the whole problem reduces to: does the right edge of that interval ever fall behind my cursor? One variable, one inequality, done. This frontier idea is the seed for Jump Game II (advance the frontier level by level to count jumps).

diagrams.title: Frontier advancing then falling behind
diagrams.caption: i is the cursor; the frontier stalls at index 3 (the 0) and the cursor overtakes it at index 4.

edgeCases.behavior: i=0 with i (0) not > farthest (0); farthest >= last (0) → returns true immediately.
i=0 sets farthest=2 ≥ last → true, even though indices 1 and 2 hold zeros (we jump over them).

pitfalls: Updating farthest BEFORE the i > farthest check — lets a stranded index slip through.
Comparing i + nums[i] without keeping the running max — a later small jump shouldn't shrink the frontier.
Forgetting nums[i] can be 0 — a 0 only fails when it's the frontier's edge and the cursor catches up.

commonMistakes: Reaching for an O(n²) DP or exponential backtracking when a single greedy frontier suffices.
Checking i > farthest after updating the frontier instead of before, letting a stranded index pass.
Assuming a 0 always fails — it only fails when you're forced to stop on it with no reach beyond.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Exponential backtracking
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Recursively trying every jump length from every index revisits the same positions and blows up exponentially, timing out on n = 10⁴.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Check order inverted in the greedy
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Updating farthest before testing i > farthest hides the stranded case — you might extend the frontier using an index you can't actually stand on.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
farthest = 0
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    farthest = max(farthest, i + x)  # updated too early
    if i > farthest:                 # now unreachable indices are masked
        return False
return True

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Letting a small jump shrink the frontier
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Assigning farthest = i + nums[i] without the max can pull the horizon backward when a later index has a small value, falsely reporting failure.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: farthest = i + nums[i]; // overwrites — loses a bigger earlier reach

followupVariations.title: Jump Game II
followupVariations.hint: Minimum jumps — same frontier, but advance level by level (BFS-style) counting each expansion.

followupVariations.title: Jump Game III
followupVariations.hint: Jumps go i±nums[i] to a zero — reachability becomes a graph BFS/DFS, not a linear frontier.

followupVariations.title: Jump Game VI
followupVariations.hint: Max score with a window of jumps — sliding-window maximum (monotonic deque) over a DP.

followupVariations.title: Gas Station
followupVariations.hint: Circular feasibility with the same 'track a running frontier and reset' greedy flavour.

patternNote: Canonical reachability-frontier greedy — collapse 'is each position good?' into one running 'farthest reachable index' and fail only when the cursor overtakes the frontier. Recognise it for line-walking feasibility questions; it generalises to Jump Game II (count jumps) and shares its frontier-and-reset spirit with Gas Station.
